name: One road at half price
brief:
A courier crosses a toll network of towns numbered 0 to `n - 1`. Each road `[a, b, cost]` in `roads` runs both ways between two different towns. The courier holds one voucher, which pays half the toll of one road, rounded down to whole pounds. The voucher is refused on any road with `src` at one end. Return the least total toll from `src` to `dst`, using the voucher on at most one road, or `-1` when `dst` cannot be reached.

Write `cheapest_with_coupon(n, roads, src, dst)`.

Example. For `n = 4`, `roads = [[0, 1, 4], [1, 3, 4], [0, 2, 1], [2, 3, 15]]`, `src = 0` and `dst = 3`, the route through town 1 costs £8 in full, or £6 with the voucher on its second road, since the first road starts at `src`. The route through town 2 costs £16, or £1 plus £7 = £8 with the voucher on the dear road. The answer is 6.
constraints: $1 \le n \le 10{,}000$ towns and at most $30{,}000$ roads, each costing £1 to £1,000,000.
$O(m \log n)$ time is the target for $m$ roads. Trying the voucher on each road in turn with a fresh search is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Run Dijkstra over pairs (town, voucher used or not). From a town with the voucher unused, each road can be paid in full, keeping the voucher, or at half, spending it. A road with `src` at one end is always paid in full.

examples.note: Halving the second £4 road on the route through town 1 gives £6; the first road starts at `src`.
Half of £7 rounds down to £3, so the route through town 1 costs £12. The direct road starts at `src`, so it stays at £13.

tests.call: cheapest_with_coupon(10000, [[i, i + 1, 1000000 - i] for i in range(9999)] + [[i, i + 2, 999990] for i in range(0, 9998, 3)], 9999, 0)

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method tries the voucher on each road in turn and runs Dijkstra again, one search per road, which runs out of time on the large networks. The step to the target is one Dijkstra over pairs (town, voucher used), so the voucher decision is made inside the search. Unlike the usual one-voucher search, the voucher is refused on any road at `src`, so the half price is offered only on other roads, and each road runs both ways.
notes: Two copies of every town, before and after the voucher, turn the choice into an ordinary shortest path; roads at `src` offer only the full toll.
Halving the dearest road of the plain cheapest route is a greedy that fails when another route has a much dearer road.
The search has $2n$ states and at most $6m$ moves, so the work is $O(m \log n)$.

planted.slip: Halving the dearest road of the plain cheapest route misses a route that is dearer in full but cheaper with the voucher.
Pricing each road only from `a` to `b` forgets that the courier may cross it from `b` to `a`.
Letting the voucher pay for a road with `src` at one end ignores the rule that the start town refuses it.
Reading the answer from the voucher-used copy of `dst` whenever it was reached forgets that the cheapest route may not spend the voucher, as when `src` is `dst`.
Trying the voucher on each road with a fresh Dijkstra is right but runs one search per road, too slow.
